title: How do you trace a request across multiple microservices (distributed tracing, correlation IDs, centralized logging)?
shortTitle: How do you trace a request across multiple microservices
keyPoints: A correlation ID is generated once at the edge and propagated everywhere so every log line across every service carries the same ID.
Distributed tracing uses trace IDs and span IDs to build a tree of operations with start/end timestamps for each hop.
Spans reveal latency contribution of each service, showing exactly which hop is slow in a Zipkin/Jaeger waterfall.
Context is propagated via the W3C traceparent header; Micrometer Tracing (formerly Sleuth) does this automatically in Spring.
Centralized logging ships all structured JSON logs to ELK or Loki, searchable by correlation ID from a single search box.
Context propagation must cross async boundaries: put trace context in Kafka message headers so the trace is not broken.
Sampling controls cost in high-volume systems; tail-based sampling keeps traces that errored or were slow.

s1_definition.oneliner: Stamp every request with a correlation ID at the edge, propagate trace and span IDs across services so a tracing tool can show the end-to-end timeline, and ship all logs to one place searchable by that ID.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Correlation ID** – a unique identifier generated at the edge and propagated through every service and log line for a request.
- **Distributed tracing** – a trace composed of spans (one per operation), linked by trace and span IDs, visualized as a waterfall in Jaeger or Zipkin.
- **Centralized logging** – shipping all services' structured logs to one searchable store like ELK so you query by correlation ID.
- **Propagation** – the W3C traceparent header carries trace context between services; Micrometer Tracing automates this in Spring.
- **Async boundaries** – trace context must be put in Kafka message headers so the trace is not broken at the queue.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a customer's loan application at National Bank of India passes through many departments: reception, verification, credit check, approval, and disbursement. If something goes wrong, you cannot figure out where unless every department stamps the same case number on the file and logs what they did. The correlation ID is that single case number. Distributed tracing is the stopwatch log showing how long the file spent at each desk. Centralized logging is the central records room where every department files a copy of its notes, all searchable by that one case number.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Distributed Tracing Flow:

  Client -> API Gateway (generate traceId=abc123)
                │
                │ traceparent: 00-abc123-gw001-01
                ▼
         Payment Service (span: pay001, parent: gw001)
                │
       ┌────────┴────────┐
       │                 │
       ▼                 ▼
  Account Svc       Kafka Message
  (span: acc001)    (traceparent in header)
  parent: pay001         │
                         ▼
                  Notification Svc
                  (span: notif001)
                  parent: pay001

  All spans share traceId=abc123
  Zipkin renders the full waterfall.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Tracing a request across microservices is about following one logical operation end to end, built on three pillars: correlation IDs, distributed tracing, and centralized logging. The correlation ID is generated once at the API gateway and propagated to every service, so every log line across the system carries the same ID. Distributed tracing adds structure with trace IDs and span IDs forming a tree with timestamps, so you see the latency contribution of each hop in a Zipkin or Jaeger waterfall.

Centralized logging ships all structured JSON logs to one searchable store like Elasticsearch. At National Bank of India, when Rajesh's transfer is slow, Pankaj pastes the correlation ID into Kibana and instantly sees every log line from every service in order. The Jaeger waterfall shows the fraud-scoring span as the clear bottleneck.

The critical detail is that context propagation must cross async boundaries. When a service publishes to Kafka, it puts the trace context in message headers so the consumer continues the same trace. Without this, the trace breaks at the queue. Sampling controls cost in high-volume systems, and tail-based sampling keeps the traces that errored or were slow.

Remember one sentence: stamp every request with a correlation ID at the edge, propagate trace and span IDs across every service including async hops, and ship all logs to one place searchable by that ID.
